Clin Infect Dis 1999; 28: 240–6. Protothecosis Protothecosis is an infection with algae of the Prototheca spp., usually P. wickerhamii. Infection occurs rarely in hu- mans but may follow minor trauma or surgery, leading to a chronic skin lesion and occasionally dissemination. Am- photericin B appears to be the most effective antifungal,1,2 and has been combined with an oral tetracycline.2 There are also case reports of itraconazole3,4 being used success- fully and fluconazole has been of benefit in a case unre- sponsive to itraconazole,5 but azole therapy has also been associated with treatment failure in a number of cases.2 Azole antifungals and surgery may be considered for pa- tients with more localised disease.1 1. Kantrow SM, Boyd AS. Protothecosis. Dermatol Clin 2003; 21: 249–55. 2. Lass-Flörl C, Mayr A. Human protothecosis. Clin Microbiol Rev 2007; 20: 230–42. 3. Tang WYM, et al. Br J Dermatol 1996; 135: 803–6. Respiratory-tract infections Pathogenic fungi may enter the body by inhalation and colonise the respiratory tract. Fungal infections of the res- piratory tract include aspergillosis, blastomycosis, coccid- ioidomycosis, cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, and para- coccidioidomycosis (see above).
